problem: End-to-end flat RL policies for embodied navigation fail on long-horizon tasks: they lack exploration guarantees, cannot backtrack, and cannot plan over long horizons. Existing hierarchical waypoint-sampling methods also degrade as the horizon grows.
motivation: Real tasks such as transport in warehouses or hospitals need deep exploration and long-horizon decisions, such as whether to return to the goal now or keep exploring for a container. Existing benchmarks like MultiON pre-specify the sub-task sequence and do not stress-test scale. The authors argue that a modular design (topological map, motion planner, and object-nav RL) transfers to harder settings when trained only on simple ones.
key_idea: A modular hierarchical transport policy uses a finite-state-machine high-level controller over Explore/Pickup/Drop. It builds a topological graph with learned exploration scores to weight frontiers, and combines A* for point goals in explored areas with an RL object-nav policy for the last mile.
insight: Modularity and a topological map with predicted-score frontier weighting generalize far better than flat RL. From default to harder, NoMap success falls from 39 to 2.8, while HTP-CNN keeps 21 and HTP-GCN 22. Weighted frontiers beat nearest-frontier: on the standard task HTP-NearestFrontier gets 52 success versus 56 (CNN) and 59 (GCN). Not all hierarchy helps: the OracleMap-Waypoints baseline is worse than flat OracleMap (Occ+Obj) in the standard setting, though it is better on the longer settings.
method: Topological graph builder: nodes are added every 2 m, each with D=12 node-direction features from a pretrained autoencoder encoder F_A on perspective RGB. Edges are added on transitions and last-visited time is stored.

Exploration score predictor F_E: a Q-learning GCN over the graph with frontier masks, or a per-frame CNN predicting scores for 3 angular sectors, trained with labels max(max_o(d_a-d_f)/5,0). Both score frontiers by their likelihood of finding objects.
Object closeness predictor F_O: a CNN on RGBD predicts a per-object closeness score, trained with labels max(1-d/5,0). It is stored per node-direction.
High-level controller: a finite state machine over {Explore, Pickup[Object], Drop} using closeness scores, hand state, and goal state. It can interrupt the current sub-task.
Weighted frontier exploration: each frontier is assigned to a parent node-direction, and the highest-F_E frontier becomes the A* goal, recomputed every step.
Pick-drop module: goes to the node with the highest closeness score using A*, orients, then hands off to a PPO-trained object-nav policy (FORWARD/TURN) that triggers pickup or drop.
Low-level controller: A* on the built occupancy map to reach point goals within explored regions.

setting.backbone: GCN or CNN exploration-score predictors, CNN closeness predictor, autoencoder encoder, PPO object-nav policy (all trained from scratch); A* planner; rule-based FSM controller
setting.training_data: 10,000 Long-HOT training configurations on 61 MP3D scenes (default level); the object-nav policy is trained with PPO for ~40M steps on 24 simulator instances; MultiON training data for the MultiON experiment
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + odometry + hand/goal state + built occupancy map
setting.action_space: high-level {Explore, Pickup, Drop}; low-level FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN ±30°, Pickup, Drop
setting.privileged: none for HTP (the oracle baselines use a GT local occupancy map and object locations)

results: On standard Long-HOT, HTP-GCN gets 59% success against 43% for NoMap and ProjNeuralMap. On the harder large-scene levels, HTP keeps 33% (hard) and 22% (harder) success while NoMap collapses to 5.2% and 2.8%. On MultiON 3-ON, HTP-GCN gets 57% success, on par with the challenge winner Lyon (57), and far above ProjNeuralMap (27).
limitations: Pickup and drop are abstracted, and objects are simple colored cylinders, so there is no physical interaction or realistic object perception.
Large-scene test scenes overlap with training scenes; the oracle-map baselines still beat HTP on the standard task; SPL is below the winner on MultiON.
Uses many hand-designed components (FSM controller, thresholds, pre-built occupancy map for A*) and is evaluated only in simulation.
